digit × base^position, added up

In base b, each digit is worth b times the digit to its right: 1101 in base 2 is 1·8 + 1·4 + 0·2 + 1·1 = 13. Bases above 10 use letters for the extra digits: A = 10, B = 11, … , F = 15 in hexadecimal.
Base b → number: read digits from the left, value = value × b + digit. Number → base b: repeatedly take value % b as the next digit from the right and divide by b; reverse at the end.

Two's complement, unsigned wrap-around, shifting bits.

A computer stores an int as 32 bits. Non-negative values are plain binary. Negative values use two's complement: −x is stored as (232 − x), which is "flip every bit of x and add 1". That is why the top bit acts as a sign, and why int runs from −231 to 231 − 1.

Logic Bit operator 1 when and (且) a & b both bits are 1 or (或) a | b at least one is 1 xor (异或) a ^ b the bits differ not (非) ~a the bit is 0

A proposition is true or false, a bit is 1 or 0. The bit operators apply and / or / not / xor to all 32 bits at once, so one integer can hold 32 true/false facts, and one operation updates all of them.
Implication "p → q" is !p || q . De Morgan: ~(a & b) == (~a | ~b) and ~ (a | b) == (~a & ~b) .

XOR cancels pairs (a ^ a = 0 , a ^ 0 = a ) and does not care about order, so XOR-ing everything leaves the one value that appears an odd number of times, in O(1) memory (P1469). The subset masks of 第10章 are these same tricks: mask >> i & 1 tests bit i.

Enumerating masks 0 … 2k − 1 tries every true/false assignment of k propositions: the brute-force way to check a logic puzzle or prove two formulas equal.

Key points to memorise
1. Base b → number: v = v × b + digit; number → base b: digits v % b, then reverse.
2. Digits above 9: A = 10 … F = 15; print with do … while so 0 shows.
3. Negative base: if r < 0, r −= b and q += 1.
4. int is 32 bits; −x = ~x + 1 (two's complement); range −2³¹ … 2³¹ − 1.
5. unsigned wraps mod 2³²; signed overflow is undefined.
7. Test bit i: x >> i & 1; set: x | 1 << i; clear: x & ~(1 << i).
8. Lowest set bit x & −x; remove it x & (x − 1).
9. XOR of all values leaves the one with odd count.
